plan.topic_summary: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) refers to cryptographic algorithms designed to remain secure against attacks by quantum computers. For a 1–5 year view, the key question is how quickly the industry can migrate from classical to quantum-resistant algorithms before cryptographically relevant quantum computers emerge, and what the performance, cost, and operational trade-offs of that migration look like.
key_questions: What is the current status of PQC standardization (e.g., NIST finalization) and which algorithm families are expected to dominate initial deployments?

What measurable performance overhead (latency, bandwidth, key size) do PQC algorithms introduce in real-world protocols such as TLS and cloud infrastructure, and how does this affect edge and IoT workloads?
How are major cloud providers, financial institutions, and government agencies sequencing their PQC migration, and what are the stated timelines?
What is the assessed severity and likelihood of 'harvest now, decrypt later' attacks on currently intercepted encrypted traffic, and which data classes are most at risk?
Will hybrid (classical + PQC) schemes become the long-term deployment model, or is a full transition to pure PQC expected within 3–5 years?
How does the realistic timeline for cryptographically relevant quantum computers affect the urgency and cost-benefit calculus of early PQC adoption?

gaps: Patent agent was not run, so there is no IP landscape or freedom-to-operate analysis; this limits conclusions about competitive moats and licensing risk but cannot be filled by paper search.
X agent was not run, so no community or practitioner sentiment signals are available; this is a limitation on gauging real-world deployment friction beyond what filings and papers show.

No science finding addresses PKI/X.509 certificate management migration (e.g., certificate size inflation, chain validation with PQC signatures), which is a major practical deployment bottleneck mentioned indirectly in market findings (M5, M7).

Several retrieved science papers are broad surveys (3 of 12), reducing the density of novel technical evidence; the specific benchmark papers (energy, comparative KEM) are the strongest but limited in number.
No evidence on PQC deployment in cloud/hyperscaler contexts (AWS, Azure, GCP), which are major migration vectors.

sources.title: Post-quantum Cryptography
Energy Consumption of Post-Quantum Cryptography on Constrained and General-Purpose Architectures
sources.venue: Gillot, O., Buchanan, W. J., & Tehrani, M. G. (2026). Energy Consumption of Post-Quantum Cryptography on Constrained and General-Purpose Architectures. Cryptography, 10(4), 55
sources.abstract: With Q-day approaching, the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) has begun, with governments across the US, UK and EU mandating migration to quantum-resistant standards. This paper benchmarks the three NIST-standardised PQC algorithms - FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) - across key generation, signing and verification operations, measuring both computational performance and energy consumption on a range of constrained IoT-class devices, from the 32-bit Raspberry Pi 1 and Zero to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi 4, as well as commodity laptop hardware. Using the FNIRSI FNB58 USB power meter and OpenSSL~3.5, results show that ML-KEM and ML-DSA achieve energy and speed efficiency comparable to classical elliptic-curve cryptography across all tested architectures. However, SLH-DSA signing is inadvisable on constrained hardware: energy costs for SLH-DSA signing on 32-bit devices were up to 243\% higher than on equivalent 64-bit hardware, making it impractical for resource-limited IoT deployments. These findings have direct implications for IoT security practitioners planning PQC migration.

sources.title: A Survey of Post-Quantum Cryptography: Start of a New Race
sources.abstract: Information security is a fundamental and urgent issue in the digital transformation era. Cryptographic techniques and digital signatures have been applied to protect and authenticate relevant information. However, with the advent of quantum computers and quantum algorithms, classical cryptographic techniques have been in danger of collapsing because quantum computers can solve complex problems in polynomial time. Stemming from that risk, researchers worldwide have stepped up research on post-quantum algorithms to resist attack by quantum computers. In this review paper, we survey studies in recent years on post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and provide statistics on the number and content of publications, including a literature overview, detailed explanations of the most common methods so far, current implementation status, implementation comparisons, and discussion on future work. These studies focused on essential public cryptography techniques and digital signature schemes, and the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) launched a competition to select the best candidate for the expected standard. Recent studies have practically implemented the public key encryption/key encapsulation mechanism (PKE/KEM) and digital signature schemes on different hardware platforms and applied various optimization measures based on other criteria. Along with the increasing number of scientific publications, the recent trend of PQC research is increasingly evident and is the general trend in the cryptography industry. The movement opens up a promising avenue for researchers in public key cryptography and digital signatures, especially on algorithms selected by NIST.

sources.title: A Comparative Performance Evaluation of Kyber, sntrup761, and FrodoKEM for Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) aims to develop cryptographic algorithms that are secure against attacks from quantum computers. This paper compares the leading postquantum cryptographic algorithms, such as Kyber, sntrup761, and FrodoKEM, in terms of their security, performance, and real-world applicability. The review highlights the strengths and weaknesses of each algorithm and provides insights into future research directions. We also discuss the challenges of transitioning from classical to post-quantum systems and the potential impacts on various industries. This paper serves as a foundation for understanding the current state of post-quantum cryptography and its future prospects in the quantum computing era.

sources.title: Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
A Survey on Post-Quantum Cryptography: State-of-the-Art and Challenges
sources.abstract: The paper explains that post-quantum cryptography is necessary due to the introduction of quantum computing causing certain algorithms to be broken. We analyze the different types of post-quantum cryptography, quantum cryptography and quantum-resistant cryptography, to provide a thorough understanding of the current solutions to the problems and their limitations. We explain the current state of quantum computing and how it has changed over time while discussing possible attacks on both types of post-quantum cryptography. Next, current post-quantum algorithms are discussed, and implementations are demonstrated. Lastly, we conclude that due to quantum cryptography's present limitations it is not a viable solution like it is often presented to be and that it is currently better to use quantum-resistant cryptography.

sources.title: Post Quantum Cryptography: A Review of Techniques, Challenges and Standardizations
sources.abstract: The development of large quantum computers will have dire consequences for cryptography. Most of the symmetric and asymmetric cryptographic algorithms are vulnerable to quantum algorithms. Grover’s search algorithm gives a square root time boost for the searching of the key in symmetric schemes like AES and 3DES. The security of asymmetric algorithms like RSA, Diffie Hellman, and ECC is based on the mathematical hardness of prime factorization and discrete logarithms. The best classical algorithms available take exponential time. Shor’s factoring algorithm can solve the problems in polynomial time. Major breakthroughs in quantum computing will render all the present-day widely used asymmetric cryptosystems insecure. This paper analyzes the vulnerability of the classical cryptosystems in the context of quantum computers, discusses various post-quantum cryptosystem families, discusses the status of the NIST post-quantum cryptography standardization process, provides a performance comparison of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms on different platforms, and finally provides a couple of future research directions in this field.

sources.title: The Mathematical Foundation of Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.abstract: On July 5, 2022, the National Institute of Standards and Technology announced four possible post-quantum cryptography standards, three of them are based on lattice theory and the other one is based on Hash function. It is well-known that the security of the lattice cryptography relies on the hardness of the shortest vector problem (SVP) and the closest vector problem (CVP). In fact, the SVP is a sphere packing problem and the CVP is a sphere covering problem. Furthermore, both SVP and CVP are equivalent to arithmetic problems of positive definite quadratic forms. This paper will briefly introduce the post-quantum cryptography and show its connections with sphere packing, sphere covering, and positive definite quadratic forms.

sources.title: Post-quantum cryptography and the quantum future of cybersecurity
sources.abstract: We review the current status of efforts to develop and deploy post-quantum cryptography on the Internet. Then we suggest specific ways in which quantum technologies might be used to enhance cybersecurity in the near future and beyond. We focus on two goals: protecting the secret keys that are used in classical cryptography, and ensuring the trustworthiness of quantum computations. These goals may soon be within reach, thanks to recent progress in both theory and experiment. This progress includes interactive protocols for testing quantumness as well as for performing uncloneable cryptographic computations; and experimental demonstrations of device-independent random number generators, device-independent quantum key distribution, quantum memories, and analog quantum simulators.

sources.title: Obfuscated Quantum and Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.venue: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC) 2026 Kobe, Japan
sources.abstract: In this work, we present an experimental deployment of a new design for combined quantum key distribution (QKD) and post-quantum cryptography (PQC). Novel to our system is the dynamic obfuscation of the QKD-PQC sequence of operations, the number of operations, and parameters related to the operations; coupled to the integration of a GPS-free quantum synchronization protocol within the QKD process. We compare the performance and overhead of our QKD-PQC system relative to a standard QKD system with one-time pad encryption, demonstrating that our design can operate in real time with little additional overhead caused by the new security features. Since our system can offer additional defensive strategies against a wide spectrum of practical attacks that undermine deployed QKD, PQC, and certain combinations of these two primitives, we suggest that our design represents one of the most secure communication systems currently available. Given the dynamic nature of its obfuscation attributes, our new system can also be adapted in the field to defeat yet-to-be-discovered practical attacks.

sources.title: Applications of Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.venue: European Conference on Cyber Warfare and Security
sources.abstract: With the constantly advancing capabilities of quantum computers, conventional cryptographic systems relying on complex math problems may encounter unforeseen vulnerabilities. Unlike regular computers, which are often deemed cost-ineffective in cryptographic attacks, quantum computers have a significant advantage in calculation speed. This distinction potentially makes currently used algorithms less secure or even completely vulnerable, compelling the exploration of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) as the most reasonable solution to quantum threats. This review aims to provide current information on applications, benefits, and challenges associated with the PQC. The review employs a systematic scoping review with the scope restricted to the years 2022 and 2023; only articles that were published in scientific journals were used in this paper. The review examined the articles on the applications of quantum computing in various spheres. However, the scope of this paper was restricted to the domain of the PQC because most of the analyzed articles featured this field. Subsequently, the paper is analyzing various PQC algorithms, including lattice-based, hash-based, code-based, multivariate polynomial, and isogeny-based cryptography. Each algorithm is being judged based on its potential applications, robustness, and challenges. All the analyzed algorithms are promising for the post-quantum era in such applications as digital signatures, communication channels, and IoT. Moreover, some of the algorithms are already implemented in the spheres of banking transactions, communication, and intellectual property. Meanwhile, despite their potential, these algorithms face serious challenges since they lack standardization, require vast amounts of storage and computation power, and might have unknown vulnerabilities that can be discovered only with years of cryptanalysis. This overview aims to give a basic understanding of the current state of post-quantum cryptography with its applications and challenges. As the world enters the quantum era, this review not only shows the need for strong security methods that can resist quantum attacks but also presents an optimistic outlook on the future of secure communications, guided by advancements in quantum technology. By bridging the gap between theoretical research and practical implementation, this paper aims to inspire further innovation and collaboration in the field.

sources.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Neural Network
sources.abstract: In recent years, quantum computers and Shor quantum algorithm have posed a threat to current mainstream asymmetric cryptography methods (e.g. RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)). Therefore, it is necessary to construct a Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) method to resist quantum computing attacks. Therefore, this study proposes a PQC-based neural network that maps a code-based PQC method to a neural network structure and enhances the security of ciphertexts with non-linear activation functions, random perturbation of ciphertexts, and uniform distribution of ciphertexts. In practical experiments, this study uses cellular network signals as a case study to demonstrate that encryption and decryption can be performed by the proposed PQC-based neural network with the uniform distribution of ciphertexts. In the future, the proposed PQC-based neural network could be applied to various applications.

sources.title: A Novel Masking Scheme with Low Additional Overhead for LWE-Based PQC Family
PDRL-PQCS: Proactive Deep Reinforcement Learning for Real-Time PQC Configuration in ITS with Edge Collaboration
sources.abstract: The emergence of quantum computing presents significant challenges for intelligent transportation systems (ITS), which rely on traditional public-key cryptography, demanding both strong security and low-latency operation. This highlights an urgent requirement for post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) algorithms to guarantee long-term protection. However, a direct integration of PQC into ITS may introduce latency and inefficiency, as static implementations cannot adapt to dynamic traffic conditions and may apply excessive security in low-risk contexts, resulting in unnecessary computational overhead, particularly within resource-constrained edge computing environments. To mitigate these issues, the PDRL-PQCS (Predictive Deep Reinforcement Learning for Post-Quantum Cryptography Selection) framework is proposed. This approach employs a Transformer-based module to generate multi-step predictions of traffic flow and computational load, thereby providing proactive contextual awareness. These predictions subsequently inform a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent, which dynamically selects optimal parameter configurations for the CRYSTALS-Kyber PQC algorithm in real time, enabling adaptive security-performance balancing across the heterogeneous nodes of an ITS edge computing network. Through this two-stage approach, PDRL-PQCS adapts PQC parameters within defined security bounds to optimally balance security assurance with operational efficiency. An extensive experimental evaluation assesses the framework under three representative traffic scenarios with diverse resource availability and congestion levels. Results indicate that PDRL-PQCS achieves 10%–20% higher overall performance compared to baseline methods across various challenging conditions.

sources.title: PQC Protection for AI Workloads - A Performance-Aware Migration Framework
sources.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence workloads have become deeply woven into healthcare, finance, defense, and critical infrastructure, and the encryption protecting those workloads now sits under a clock. A sufficiently capable quantum computer running Shor's algorithm will break the asymmetric cryptography - RSA, Elliptic Curve Cryptography, and Diffie-Hellman - that guard data in transit and the roots of trust behind device and model authentication. The threat is not confined to some distant future either. Adversaries are already intercepting and storing encrypted traffic under a “harvest now, decrypt later” strategy, betting that quantum hardware will catch up before the data loses its value. This paper studies what actually happens when we move AI workloads onto the post-quantum algorithms that the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) finalized in 2024, namely ML-KEM for key establishment and ML-DSA for digital signatures. We frame the problem specifically for heterogeneous compute platforms - the mix of general-purpose cores, GPU accelerators, embedded controllers, and system-on-chip (SoC) endpoints on which modern AI is deployed - because these environments carry latency budgets, memory ceilings, and signature-size constraints that generic cryptographic benchmarks tend to ignore. Using a controlled experimental design that compares a classical baseline, a pure post-quantum configuration, and a hybrid configuration across transformer inference, distributed training, and federated learning, we characterize the overhead these algorithms introduce and where it concentrates. We then translate those measurements into a practical, phased migration framework that maps workload classes to cryptographic strategies and sequences the transition to preserve operational continuity. The central finding is that post-quantum protection for AI is far less a raw performance problem than an engineering and governance problem: symmetric encryption already survives quantum attack, key exchange migrates with negligible cost, and the real difficulty lies in the larger signatures and longer-lived roots of trust that authentication depends on. The proposed framework gives engineering leaders a concrete way to prioritize, sequence, and verify the migration on the heterogeneous platforms where AI actually runs.

sources.title: Operationalising Post Quantum TLS Automated Configuration Profiling and Hybrid PQC Deployment in Financial Infrastructure
sources.abstract: Organisations are upgrading their cryptographic infrastructure to become quantum safe before large scale quantum computers materialise. Post quantum cryptography (PQC) standards now exist for key exchange and digital signatures, but the urgent question for adopters is how to operationalise PQC in complex environments with confidence. In banking, Transport Layer Security (TLS), for example, protects data in transit across public facing channels and internal services, and is terminated at many heterogeneous endpoints (web servers, API gateways, load balancers, reverse proxies), each a potential quantum vulnerable component and migration target. We argue that the bottleneck is operational rather than algorithmic, hybrid key exchanges such as MLKEM and hybrid MLKEM key exchanges are already available in mainstream libraries, but security teams lack precise visibility into TLS configurations and repeatable methods for enabling PQC compatible settings across a heterogeneous estate. This paper presents a configuration parsing methodology that automatically extracts and normalises TLS cryptographic posture across dominant enterprise web server stacks, producing a unified, provenance traced cryptographic inventory as a foundation for migration and compliance. We demonstrate the approach on 8,443 real world Nginx configurations from public repositories and in a proof of concept deployment at a financial institution, where MLKEM and hybrid MLKEM key exchanges at TLS termination points (web server and API gateway) securing an internal application, with zero application layer changes and manageable performance overhead.

sources.title: Exploration of PQC-Based Digital Signature Schemes in TLS Certificates
sources.venue: The Asian Bulletin of Big Data Management
sources.abstract: The rapid development in quantum computers brings huge risks to traditional cryptographic systems. This paper talks about the integration of PQC-based digital signature schemes to solve challenges posed on Transport Layer Security certificates. In this paper, we give an analysis of the efficacy, security, and performance implications of various schemes in PQC—particularly lattice-based, hash-based, and multivariate polynomial-based algorithms. We detail more closely the challenges of the real deployment, directly connected with these digital signatures, considering communication overhead and computational costs. Our findings indicate that hybrid certificate chains, which integrate multiple PQC schemes, offer a feasible solution for a seamless transition to quantum-resistant standards with manageable performance trade-offs. Moreover, our study extends to the quantification of security benefits these PQC schemes provide against both quantum and classical computational attacks, underscoring their potential in enhancing the resilience of digital communication systems. This paper aims to contribute valuable insights to ongoing standardization discussions and support the broader adoption of PQC, thereby ensuring robust and future-proof security in digital communications amidst the advancing quantum computing era.

sources.title: SoK: PQC PAKEs Design, Security and Performance
sources.abstract: Password Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE) establishes secure communication channels using passwords for authentication. Currently, standardized PAKEs rely on classical asymmetric cryptography. However, these PAKEs may become insecure should the expected quantum threat become a reality. Despite the growing interest in realizing quantum-safe PAKEs, they did not receive much attention from the ongoing Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) integration efforts. Hence, there is a significant awareness gap compared to PQC primitives subject to the official standardization processes. We provide a comprehensive overview of existing PQC PAKEs, classify their design rationales and authentication methods, and address aspects related to their security and performance. We identify PAKE designs that are still unexplored in the PQC realm and discuss the possibility of their adaptation. Thus, we offer a detailed reference for future work on PQC PAKEs.

sources.title: Practical hybrid PQC-QKD protocols with enhanced security and performance
sources.abstract: Quantum resistance is vital for emerging cryptographic systems as quantum technologies continue to advance towards large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Resistance may be offered by quantum key distribution (QKD), which provides information-theoretic security using quantum states of photons, but may be limited by transmission loss at long distances. An alternative approach uses classical means and is conjectured to be resistant to quantum attacks, so-called post-quantum cryptography (PQC), but it is yet to be rigorously proven, and its current implementations are computationally expensive. To overcome the security and performance challenges present in each, here we develop hybrid protocols by which QKD and PQC inter-operate within a joint quantum-classical network. In particular, we consider different hybrid designs that may offer enhanced speed and/or security over the individual performance of either approach. Furthermore, we present a method for analyzing the security of hybrid protocols in key distribution networks. Our hybrid approach paves the way for joint quantum-classical communication networks, which leverage the advantages of both QKD and PQC and can be tailored to the requirements of various practical networks.

sources.title: Integrating PQC into standard industry protocols
sources.venue: Brno University of Technology Digital Library (Brno University of Technology)
sources.abstract: Tato diplomová práce se zabývá možnostmi integrace postkvantové kryptografie do pro- tokolů a systémů využívaných v průmyslovém prostředí a v prostředí infrastruktury veřej- ných klíčů. V teoretické části jsou popsány systémy infrastruktury veřejných klíčů, certi- fikáty standardu X.509 a moderní kryptografické algoritmy včetně postkvantové krypto- grafie. Dále jsou analyzovány protokoly EST, SCEP, LoRaWAN a ACME, u nichž byly identifikovány kryptografické mechanismy a možnosti jejich nahrazení za kvantově odolné varianty. S ohledem na infrastrukturu veřejných klíčů pak byly prozkoumány některé ve- řejně dostupné systémy pro management PKI a z nich byl vybrán systém LamassuIoT pro integraci postkvantové ochrany do jeho mechanismů distribuce certifikátů. Implementace byla zaměřena na proces distribuce certifikátů pomocí protokolu EST v systému Lamas- suIoT. Systém byl rozšířen o podporu podpisového schématu ML-DSA a komunikační proces protokolu EST byl převeden na hybridní výměnu klíče ML-KEM-768+X25519. Funkčnost byla ověřena pomocí klientské sady na STM32. Výsledná konfigurace byla změřena a naměřené hodnoty ukazují dopad kvantově odolných kryptografických algo- ritmů na provozní vlastnosti systému. Naměřené hodnoty byly srovnány s teoretickým odhadem založeným na údajích uvedených v oficiálních specifikacích algoritmů. Měření dopadu na výkon bylo provedeno, ale jeho výsledky neprokázaly zásadní zvýšení výpočetní náročnosti na straně serveru.

sources.title: Navigating the NIST PQC Standards: Trade-offs and Case Studies
sources.abstract: The rapid advancement of quantum computing poses a significant threat to classical cryptographic systems, particularly to widely used public-key schemes that rely on integer factorisation and the discrete logarithm problem. To ensure long-term data security against potential quantum adversaries, post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is currently standardised by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). This paper goes beyond a theoretical overview by employing a systematic methodology to evaluate the empirical performance trade-offs of the newly standardised algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA) and key finalists (FN-DSA and HQC). Based on a comprehensive review of fragmented performance data, the work presents a comparative analysis focusing on data overhead, computational latency, and resource efficiency. As a primary contribution, this study proposes a deployment-oriented taxonomy that explicitly maps these PQC standards to optimal practical use cases, considering diverse constraints across Internet of Things, cloud environments, and blockchain networks. Furthermore, the paper addresses critical real-world deployment challenges, such as vulnerabilities to side-channel attacks and hardware-level implementation constraints. Ultimately, this work systematises current knowledge into a unified decision-making framework, guiding system architects in complex migration towards a quantum-resilient digital ecosystem.

sources.title: On the Security Implications of PQC in TLS: Handshake Exhaustion and IDS Degradation
sources.abstract: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is increasingly being integrated into TLS 1.3 to enhance resilience against quantum-enabled attacks. However, the additional computational and communication overhead introduced by PQC primitives during the handshake phase may also amplify the impact of TLS handshake exhaustion attacks, leading to more severe Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) threats. In this study, we establish an empirical testbed consisting of one PQC-enabled TLS server and ten attacking nodes, generating over 16.5 GB of mixed traffic data that includes both legitimate browsing behavior and high-intensity handshake exhaustion attacks. Experimental results show that PQC-TLS can prolong periods of sustained high CPU utilization on the server by up to 88 times, significantly amplifying the effectiveness of such attacks. Furthermore, we evaluate state-of-the-art deep learning-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) and observe a substantial decline in attack detection performance under PQC traffic conditions. In particular, exosphere achieves only around 50% recall, while HyperVision's AU-ROC degrades to near-random levels (0.49), revealing critical detection blind spots in existing IDS when operating in PQC environments. The main contributions of this work are threefold: (1) we systematically quantify and analyze the root causes of IDS detection blind spots in PQC settings; (2) we publicly release a comprehensive PQC-DDoS hybrid traffic dataset, including precise attack timestamps and server-side resource monitoring data; and (3) we open-source all experimental code and AWS deployment scripts, enabling a fully reproducible cloud-based testing environment. These resources aim to support both academia and industry in developing next-generation PQC-aware intrusion detection systems.

sources.title: NoisePQC++: A Unified NIST-Compliant PQC and Hybrid-PQC Implementation of the Noise Protocol
sources.abstract: The threat of quantum computers to classical public-key cryptography has created an urgent need to evolve secure communication protocols with post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) primitives. The Noise Protocol Framework, widely used in systems such as WireGuard and WhatsApp, traditionally relies on the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) public-key exchange scheme, which is vulnerable to quantum threats. In this paper, we present NoisePQC++, a unified C++23 implementation of the Noise Protocol framework augmented with post-quantum Key Encapsulation Mechanisms and Hybrid Forward Secrecy. Our design integrates the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) standardized ML-KEM algorithm alongside classical ECDH, enabling full PQC, hybrid ECDH+PQC handshakes, and unified support for all 57 classical Noise handshake pattern variants, 13 post-quantum Noise handshakes, and their hybrid variants. Compared with prior work, NoisePQC++ offers broader protocol coverage, more complete implementation support, and greater flexibility. Our evaluation shows minimal overhead under normal network conditions and acceptable overhead in adverse cases, while significantly improving resistance against quantum adversaries. These results indicate that NIST-standardized post-quantum and hybrid Noise handshakes are practical and provide a credible basis for future deployment.

sources.title: Secure Computation After Quantum: PQC, Confidential Clouds, and Policy-Grade Auditability
sources.venue: International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)
sources.abstract: Abstract: This study investigates how secure computation can remain trustworthy during the post-quantum transition, in which large-scale quantum computation threatens the public-key primitives used for key exchange, authentication, and software trust. The analysis treats quantum readiness as a systems property rather than a cryptographic substitution exercise. In practical deployments, cryptographic migrations change protocol sizes and performance characteristics, while cloud execution substrates introduce privileged attack surfaces that can expose data despite formally strong cryptography. A unified architecture is proposed that couples standardised post-quantum cryptography (PQC) for key establishment and digital signatures with confidential cloud execution (hardware-backed isolation and remote attestation) and with policy-grade auditability implemented via policy-as-code plus cryptographic provenance. The evaluation uses real, published parameter sizes from standardised PQC algorithms and real published performance measurements for trusted execution environments to quantify bandwidth overhead, handshake expansion, and the capacity impact of protected execution. The results show that PQC adoption can introduce substantial protocol-layer size expansion, with digital signature payloads frequently dominating bandwidth budgets relative to key encapsulation. Hybrid deployment profiles increase overhead further because classical and post-quantum materials are transmitted together, supporting staged rollouts with explicit deprecation timelines. Confidential computing reduces exposure to compromised hypervisors but imposes workload-sensitive overheads, motivating selective isolation of high-value computations combined with continuous, evidence-centric governance. Keywords post-quantum cryptography; confidential computing; trusted execution environments; policy-as-code; auditability; attestation; cryptographic agility; compliance; secure computation; zero trust.

findings.claim: PQC-enabled TLS handshakes may amplify handshake-exhaustion DDoS attacks. In one testbed, server CPU stayed highly loaded for up to 88 times longer.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is an arXiv preprint and not peer reviewed. The testbed is small (one server, ten attacking nodes). The abstract does not say which PQC parameters or hardware were used, so generalisation is uncertain.
findings.supporting_excerpt: PQC-TLS can prolong periods of sustained high CPU utilization on the server by up to 88 times

findings.claim: Deep-learning intrusion detection systems degrade sharply on PQC traffic. One system reached near-random AU-ROC, which suggests a security blind spot during migration.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The result comes from a single preprint with a specific dataset and specific IDS models. It is not independently replicated. The abstract does not say whether retraining on PQC traffic would fix the problem.
findings.supporting_excerpt: HyperVision's AU-ROC degrades to near-random levels (0.49)

findings.claim: PQC raises bandwidth and handshake size. Signature payloads are the main cost, and hybrid (classical plus PQC) deployments add more. This is a structural cost for constrained networks and devices.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The evidence is mainly a review or analysis built on published parameter sizes, not new measurements. src_9987e02f40 also flags latency, memory and signature-size constraints on heterogeneous AI platforms, but its abstract is truncated. The sources support the direction of the overhead, not its magnitude in production.
findings.supporting_excerpt: digital signature payloads frequently dominating bandwidth budgets relative to key encapsulation

findings.claim: The papers disagree on overhead. Some report minimal or manageable cost, while others report severe amplification under attack or large size expansion. The measured penalty seems to depend heavily on workload, threat model and hardware, and no common benchmark reconciles the results.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: src_93fbebde13 reports minimal overhead under normal conditions, and src_971eca27d6 (a thesis) found no major increase in server compute. src_360d24bdaa calls trade-offs manageable. src_ae754525d8 reports 88x CPU persistence under attack, and src_36248af4c5 reports substantial size expansion. Several of these are preprints or low-citation works with small, setup-specific tests. The apparent conflict may reflect different scenarios rather than true contradiction.

findings.claim: Side-channel attacks and hardware-level implementation constraints are open deployment risks for the NIST PQC algorithms. Masking countermeasures for lattice (LWE) schemes are an active research area, which suggests protection has a cost.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: src_10a7c54025 names side-channel vulnerabilities as a real-world challenge. src_85fc0e903a has only a title and no abstract, so the claim that masking carries overhead is inferred from the title alone. The papers give no data on how severe the exposure is.

findings.claim: Migration may be limited more by operations than by algorithms. Organisations lack visibility into TLS configurations across heterogeneous estates, which makes inventory and repeatable enablement hard.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is an arXiv preprint. The sample is Nginx configs from public repositories, which may not represent enterprise estates, plus one financial-institution proof of concept. The 'operational bottleneck' is the authors' own argument.
findings.supporting_excerpt: security teams lack precise visibility into TLS configurations and repeatable methods for enabling PQC compatible settings across a heterogeneous estate.

findings.claim: The security of PQC is conjectured, not rigorously proven, and implementations are computationally expensive. The authors present QKD as a possible complement, but it has its own limit of transmission loss over distance. Both routes carry unresolved limits.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a preprint that frames the problem to motivate its own hybrid protocols, so the framing may be favourable to that approach. The abstract gives no quantitative evidence on cost or on cryptanalysis progress.
findings.supporting_excerpt: but it is yet to be rigorously proven, and its current implementations are computationally expensive

findings.claim: Coverage of PQC is uneven. Password-authenticated key exchange (PAKE) has received little attention in migration efforts, so some protocol classes may lack mature quantum-safe options.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single survey (SoK) abstract. It identifies an awareness gap and unexplored designs. It does not show that the gap causes security failures.
findings.supporting_excerpt: they did not receive much attention from the ongoing Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) integration efforts.

findings.claim: Adaptive, learned selection of PQC parameters, such as the DRL approach for Kyber in ITS, may add complexity and attack surface. The abstract shows no adversarial or security-downgrade analysis.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The abstract is truncated and the evaluation results are not visible. The absence of a security-downgrade analysis in the visible text is a gap, not proof of a flaw. The security bounds the authors mention are not described.

hype_flags: 'Harvest now, decrypt later' described as already occurring (src_9987e02f40): the abstract gives no evidence for this, and nothing in the papers dates when a quantum computer capable of breaking RSA or ECC will exist.
'Future-proof' or 'robust' security claims (src_360d24bdaa): PQC hardness is conjectured (src_6a33060056), and side-channel exposure remains (src_10a7c54025).
'Minimal overhead' and 'practical' handshakes (src_93fbebde13): measured under normal network conditions, while src_ae754525d8 shows large degradation under attack.
'Manageable trade-offs' for hybrid certificate chains (src_360d24bdaa): this sits against reported size expansion and added hybrid overhead (src_36248af4c5).
Framing PQC migration as mainly an algorithm swap: src_8b5ec17baf and src_36248af4c5 point to operational and systems-level barriers.

finding.claim: S2 generalises beyond what was tested. The 'constrained IoT-class' hardware is Raspberry Pi 1, Zero and 4 plus a laptop, running OpenSSL 3.5. It does not include microcontroller-class devices. The 'comparable to elliptic-curve cryptography' result comes from a single preprint and covers only energy and speed, so it should not be read as general parity with classical ECC on constrained devices.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract documents a narrow hardware set (Linux-capable single-board computers and a laptop). Only the abstract was reviewed, so any further caveats in the paper are not visible. The finding should state this scope and that it rests on a single preprint.
finding.supporting_excerpt: measuring both computational performance and energy consumption on a range of constrained IoT-class devices, from the 32-bit Raspberry Pi 1 and Zero to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi 4, as well as commodity laptop hardware.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S2 and S12 frame PQC cost as an energy and speed trade-off on resource-limited devices. This leaves out server-side and network costs that other retrieved papers measure. PQC-enabled TLS may amplify handshake-exhaustion DDoS, and signature payloads and hybrid modes expand bandwidth. A 'comparable to ECC' headline can therefore mislead about deployment cost.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The 88x figure comes from one preprint testbed. It still contradicts a benign reading of S2 under attack conditions. src_36248af4c5 separately reports that signature payloads dominate bandwidth and hybrid profiles increase overhead. Both are costs that S2's energy and speed metrics do not capture.
finding.supporting_excerpt: PQC-TLS can prolong periods of sustained high CPU utilization on the server by up to 88 times, significantly amplifying the effectiveness of such attacks.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S1 is labelled verified_fact, but the statement that US, UK and EU governments are 'mandating' migration is an introductory assertion in one preprint's abstract. No policy document was retrieved to verify it. The abstract also carries an anomalous future publication date (2026-10-19). S1 should be downgraded or sourced to the actual mandates.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract establishes only that the authors assert this. It does not establish the scope or force of the mandates, or that they are what drives migration. Verification would need primary policy sources, which are absent from the evidence.
finding.supporting_excerpt: with governments across the US, UK and EU mandating migration to quantum-resistant standards.

finding.claim: S4 gives an incomplete and dated picture of the standardised families. The cited abstract describes a July 2022 announcement of four candidates, three lattice and one hash-based. It is not a statement about the final FIPS 203/204/205 set. Another retrieved paper lists HQC (a code-based scheme) and FN-DSA as further key algorithms. 'Hash-based the other main selected family' omits code-based selection.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The cited source is a 2022 snapshot of candidates. src_10a7c54025 names 'key finalists (FN-DSA and HQC)', so code-based schemes are part of the standards landscape. The abstract does not say HQC's formal status, so this caveat is moderate.
finding.supporting_excerpt: On July 5, 2022, the National Institute of Standards and Technology announced four possible post-quantum cryptography standards, three of them are based on lattice theory and the other one is based on Hash function.

finding.claim: S11's 'bifurcation' of the field is likely an artefact of the small retrieved sample. It ignores a third strand visible in the risk search: deployment-security and operational studies. These cover handshake-exhaustion DDoS, IDS blind spots, TLS inventory and configuration problems, side channels and protocol-coverage gaps (PAKE). The claim that the field splits into benchmarking and immature hybrids is not supported by a systematic sample.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt is from src_8b5ec17baf. A handful of search hits cannot show the structure of a field. Papers on operations, attack surface and coverage gaps do not fit either of S11's two buckets. This weakens the generalisation 'across this sample'.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We argue that the bottleneck is operational rather than algorithmic

finding.claim: S7 and the surrounding findings treat PQC's security as settled, with only deployment feasibility as the open issue. Retrieved work states that PQC security is conjectured rather than proven. Implementation-level risks such as side channels and masking costs are also active concerns. The findings never state the residual cryptanalytic and implementation risk of the standardised algorithms.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: This is a general gap rather than a refutation. The statement comes from a preprint arguing for hybrid PQC-QKD, so it is partisan. src_10a7c54025 separately flags side-channel vulnerabilities and hardware-level constraints. Both bear on how S7's 'more viable path' conclusion should be read.
finding.supporting_excerpt: but it is yet to be rigorously proven, and its current implementations are computationally expensive.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S7 rests on a single non-peer-reviewed arXiv survey's conclusion and is stated without qualification. Other retrieved work argues QKD and PQC are complementary and combines them (S8), so the QKD-versus-PQC verdict is contested rather than established.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The finding correctly says 'at least one paper argues', but it omits that the position conflicts with hybrid-approach papers. Both sides are only abstract-level evidence.
finding.supporting_excerpt: we conclude that due to quantum cryptography's present limitations it is not a viable solution like it is often presented to be

limitations: Only titles and abstracts were available. Several abstracts are truncated, and src_85fc0e903a has no abstract, so the numbers and conclusions behind many claims could not be checked.
Only 12 papers were retrieved, and many are low-citation, newly published or preprints (arXiv, Research Square) that are not peer reviewed.

There is no evidence in the set on quantum hardware timelines, cryptanalysis of the NIST standards, supply-chain or single-vendor dependence, or cost data. Absence of such evidence here is a coverage gap, not evidence of safety or risk.
Experiments are mostly small testbeds or proofs of concept, such as one financial institution, one STM32 client and one ten-node attack setup. Results may not generalise.
src_971eca27d6 is a Czech-language thesis, read from its abstract only, and its measurement details are not visible.
Search results skew toward TLS and protocol integration, so hardware, embedded and side-channel risks are underrepresented.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were reviewed. Caveats or methods in the full papers may soften or strengthen the challenges.
Several evidence items are single preprints or have zero citations. These include the 88x DDoS result and the IDS degradation result, so they are suggestive rather than established.
The evidence set is a small retrieved sample, so claims about the field's overall structure or about standards status cannot be fully checked.
No primary policy or NIST documents were retrieved, so the mandate and standardisation-status points are flagged as unverified rather than refuted.
S5, S6, S8, S9 and S10 were left unchallenged because they are narrow and consistent with the abstracts cited.

draft.summary: The evidence shows a field in rapid research expansion (exact-phrase papers rising from 847 in 2024 to 1,913 in 2025, +125.9% YoY) around three NIST-standardised algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) whose energy and speed on tested 32/64-bit platforms is reported comparable to classical ECC for key establishment and signing, except SLH-DSA signing on 32-bit hardware (S1-S3). Risk and challenge findings materially qualify this: the 'constrained' hardware tested was Raspberry Pi-class, not microcontrollers (C1), server-side, bandwidth and DDoS-amplification costs are measured elsewhere (R1, R3, C2), PQC security is described as conjectured rather than proven (R7, C6), and side-channel, PAKE-coverage and operational-inventory gaps remain open (R5, R6, R8). On the commercial side, PQC appears in SEC filings from network security vendors, an application-delivery vendor, a telecom and banks (M1, M2, M4, M5, M7), but these are product-marketing and risk statements, not evidence of paying customer adoption, and Cisco itself flags failure to drive adoption as a risk (M3). No patent evidence, no social/X evidence and no price-and-timing evidence were available in this version, and the Company Scout list is dominated by micro-cap filers with negligible or declining revenue whose PQC claims should be treated with heavy caution (K1, K4, K5). The main uncertainty is not whether PQC standards exist but how quickly heterogeneous estates migrate, at what operating cost, and with what residual cryptanalytic and implementation risk.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Evidence for the next 12 months is limited to vendor product statements (M1, M2, M4, M5) and one explicit adoption risk (M3). No customer-deployment, revenue or pricing evidence exists, and the operational findings suggest inventory and configuration, not algorithm choice, is the near-term bottleneck (R6). Banks citing legacy-system complexity (M7) indicate migration stretches beyond this window for some sectors.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Nothing in the retrieved evidence speaks directly to 3-5 year outcomes; the findings support only that standards exist and hybrid deployment is being studied (S1, S8). Long-run value depends on whether cryptanalytic and implementation risk is reduced (R7, R5) and whether adoption actually occurs (M3), neither of which the evidence resolves.

bull.label: ai_interpretation
bull.narrative: PQC standards are finalised and the literature has shifted toward benchmarking real migration on real platforms, with ML-KEM and ML-DSA reported as broadly comparable to classical ECC in energy and speed on tested hardware (S1, S2). Vendors across networking, application delivery and telecom already describe quantum-safe products and PQC certificates in regulatory filings (M1, M2, M4, M5), and the topic appears across banking and insurance filings as a general enterprise risk item (M10, M7). A standards-driven, compliance-shaped refresh cycle could therefore pull through on a multi-year horizon.

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: Migration proceeds, but the binding constraints are operational and cost-related rather than algorithmic. Organisations lack visibility into TLS configurations across heterogeneous estates (R6), PQC signature payloads and hybrid modes expand bandwidth (R3), PQC-enabled TLS can amplify handshake-exhaustion attacks and intrusion detection degrades on PQC traffic (R1, R2), and SLH-DSA signing is impractical on constrained 32-bit devices (S3). The 'comparable to ECC' result was measured on Raspberry Pi-class hardware, not microcontrollers (C1), so parity claims should not be generalised. Value accrues to vendors with existing installed estates rather than as a step change in demand.

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The case can fail on three fronts. First, security is asserted rather than proven: PQC security is described as conjectured and implementations are computationally expensive (R7), and the findings never state residual cryptanalytic risk (C6). Second, the measured penalty depends heavily on workload, threat model and hardware, with no common benchmark reconciling 'minimal cost' against 'severe amplification' reports (R4). Third, adoption may simply not happen on schedule - Cisco explicitly flags failure to implement or drive customer adoption as a risk (M3) - and protocol classes such as PAKE lack mature quantum-safe options (R8). The name-level evidence is also weak: the only company filings specifically centred on PQC include micro-cap filers with negligible revenue and negative growth (M8, K1, K4, K5).

limitations: This is a research assessment for a 1-5 year view, not investment advice; it contains no price targets, entry points, timing signals or buy/sell/hold recommendations.
Every statement is bounded by the cited findings; where no finding exists the item was placed in missing_data rather than inferred.

The research-activity metric is an exact-phrase OpenAlex count, excludes synonyms and abbreviations, is not normalised for overall publishing growth, and excludes the partial current year; it measures academic attention only, not commercial success (rule 7).
Several findings rest on single preprints or arXiv surveys with low confidence, and the challenge findings C1-C7 materially weaken S1, S2, S4, S7, S11 and S12; confidence is set accordingly.
Market evidence is drawn from SEC filing excerpts describing capabilities and risks, which is not proof that customers buy, deploy or pay for the technology (rule 6).

The M8 and K1/K4/K5 company mentions come from micro-cap filings with negligible or negative revenue and, for M8, a promotional-sounding claim; Company Scout next-runner scores are transparent heuristics, not predictions of returns, and smaller companies carry more risk and less disclosure.
Headline-based findings, if any existed, would be unverified claims; no X findings were provided at all in this version.
No patent, social or price evidence was available, so the assessment under-represents intellectual-property positioning, near-term catalysts and timing risk.

dimensions.label: Research Momentum
dimensions.rationale: Code-computed OpenAlex counts of works containing the exact phrase rise from 265 (2020) to 847 (2024) and 1,913 (2025), a 125.9% YoY increase, and the retrieved findings show the literature spanning benchmarking, protocol integration, side channels and hybrid QKD-PQC work (S1-S12, R1-R9). Caveat: the count is exact-phrase only, not synonym-normalised and not adjusted for overall publishing growth, and high paper volume is not evidence of commercial success (rule 7).

dimensions.label: Technical Feasibility
dimensions.rationale: The standards are finalised and benchmarked for real migration (S1, S4), and ML-KEM/ML-DSA are reported energy- and speed-comparable to classical ECC on the tested hardware (S2). This is offset by SLH-DSA signing being impractical on constrained 32-bit devices (S3), telemetry showing server CPU loaded up to 88 times longer in one PQC-TLS testbed (R1), structural bandwidth growth from signatures and hybrids (R3), contested security proof status (R7) and open side-channel work (R5).

dimensions.label: Commercial Readiness
dimensions.rationale: Multiple vendors already describe quantum-safe products in SEC filings: Fortinet within FortiOS (M1), Cisco in AI-ready switches (M2), F5 in application delivery and security (M4), and Chunghwa Telecom lists PQC certificates among its cybersecurity offerings (M5). Readiness is product-level only: no filing quantifies PQC revenue, and one large bank frames migration as complex because of legacy systems (M7).

dimensions.label: Customer Adoption
dimensions.rationale: The evidence is about product marketing and risk framing, not adoption. Cisco flags failure to timely implement or drive customer adoption as a risk that could expose pre-quantum data (M3), and a large bank describes migration as complex due to legacy systems and interdependencies (M7). No finding reports a deployed customer, contract or adoption metric.

dimensions.label: Industry Investment
dimensions.rationale: No finding quantifies investment specifically in PQC. Indirect signals are company-level R&D intensity from Company Scout (F5 at 17.5% of revenue, Cisco at 15.1%) (K2, K3) and PQC appearing across sectors in filings (M10, M7); none of this isolates PQC spending, so this is a weak, low-confidence rating rather than a measured one.

dimensions.label: Competitive Position
dimensions.rationale: Filings identify participants (Fortinet M1, Cisco M2, F5 M4, Chunghwa M5), and among the configured cybersecurity companies only Fortinet's retrieved excerpt mentions PQC (M9). There is no evidence of market share, differentiation, win rates or pricing, and the Company Scout scores are explicitly heuristics, not rankings of competitive strength.

dimensions.label: Supply-Chain Readiness
dimensions.rationale: Constrained-device supply-chain readiness is not directly measured. The relevant evidence is that SLH-DSA signing is impractical on resource-constrained devices and 32-bit costs are substantially higher than 64-bit (S3), parity claims exclude microcontroller-class hardware (C1), signature and hybrid payloads expand bandwidth (R3), and organisations lack visibility into TLS configurations across heterogeneous estates (R6). These point to immature supply-chain readiness for embedded PQC.

notes: Weights are initial assumptions, not fitted to data. The score is an explainable heuristic, not a validated prediction of stock performance.
Sources are de-duplicated by URL/DOI/title. A single announcement reported by several outlets is not yet merged into one event.
Confidence lowered to 'low': coverage is 90%, but the cited ratings themselves are mostly of lower confidence.
score.formula: base = sum(weight x rating/5) / sum(weight of evidenced dimensions) x 100; score = base x (1 - max_penalty x risk_rating/5). Dimensions without cited findings are 'missing', not zero.
